The Tropical royal flycatcher (Onychorhynchus coronatus) is a distinctive passerine of Neotropical lowland forests, and its life history reveals several notable features. Eggs are incubated at a stable temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], and under these thermal conditions, the incubation period averages 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days], a duration that is quite typical for a bird of its body size. Notably, the eggs are incubated for only about 60 percent of the daylight hours, meaning the adult does not sit continuously but leaves the nest periodically. Neonates emerge with a very modest body mass, weighing just 1.76 grams [Wwb = 1.76 grams] at hatching. This altricial condition is characteristic of tyrant flycatchers, and the chicks are entirely dependent on both parents for brooding and provisioning during their first critical days of life. The low birth weight stands in contrast to the ultimate size the birds will attain as fully grown adults.

Adult body mass in this species shows marked sexual dimorphism, a pattern commonly observed among tropical forest birds. Males, however, are substantially larger, with an ultimate wet weight reaching approximately 21.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 21.8 grams]. This size difference likely influences behavioral roles during the breeding season, as the larger males may be more adept at defending territories while the females undertake much of the nest construction and incubation duties. The dimorphism is consistent with that seen in other members of the Onychorhynchus genus, where males tend to be heavier and possess more elaborate crest plumage used in courtship displays.

The species exhibits a relatively slow pace of life for a small passerine, particularly in terms of its schedule of development and reproduction. Under the warm conditions typical of its lowland habitat, approximately 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a predictable sequence of ontogenetic milestones unfolds. This extended juvenile period is an important component of the species' life history strategy.

The first reproductive event for an individual is typically deferred until a relatively advanced age, reflecting the time needed to secure a high-quality territory and find a mate. The time since birth at first brood has been reported as 438 days since birth [tR = 438 days since birth], under the same ambient conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This delayed first breeding is a common pattern among Neotropical insectivores that experience low rates of adult mortality. The annual reproductive output is also constrained; females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and field observations indicate that they typically produce about 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 2 clutches per year], resulting in a maximum rate of 2 eggs per year. This low fecundity is offset by relatively high adult survival rates.

The maximum basal metabolic rate, measured under controlled laboratory conditions using flow-through respirometry, reaches 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This value is consistent with the allometric expectations for a passerine of its adult body mass. In terms of lifespan, the oldest documented individuals in field studies have attained a maximum longevity of about 2810 days [am = about 2810 days], when living under the warm thermal conditions of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively long lifespan, combined with deferred first reproduction and low fecundity, places the Tropical royal flycatcher firmly on the slow end of the life history continuum among Neotropical passerines, a strategy that appears well-suited to the stable, low-mortality environment of mature lowland forests.
